subtopics.title: The People of Ghana
learningGoals: Trace the original homes and movement patterns of the major ethnic groups in Ghana
Assess the factors and impact of the migration of the major ethnic groups into Ghana
Recount the factors for the rise and decline of the major states and kingdoms in Ghana
Discuss the roles of matriarchs and patriarchs of the major kingdoms and states in precolonial Ghana
subtopics.keyConceptSummary: Ghana's major ethnic groups — including the Gonja, Mole-Dagbani, Guan, Akan, Ewe, and Ga-Adangbe — originally settled in different parts of West Africa before migrating to their present locations. Over time, some of these groups formed powerful states and kingdoms, led by patriarchs and matriarchs whose leadership shaped Ghana's early history.

subtopics.keyConceptSummary: The environment includes everything around us — land, water, air, and living things. Environmental challenges, such as pollution, often result from human activities and can have serious effects on communities if not properly managed.

subtopics.title: Resources in Ghana
learningGoals: Explain what resources mean
Identify the various types of resources
Identify types of natural resources (renewable and non-renewable)
Discuss the importance of resources in Ghana
Discuss ways of developing resources in Ghana and the challenges involved
subtopics.keyConceptSummary: Resources are things people use to meet their needs — some, like forests and water, are renewable because they can replenish over time, while others, like minerals, are non-renewable. Ghana has many natural resources that are important to its development, but managing them sustainably comes with real challenges.

subtopics.title: Political Institutions and Structures in Ghana
learningGoals: Analyse indigenous political systems in precolonial Ghana and their relevance today
Compare and contrast different forms of political systems in precolonial Ghana
Examine the nature of modern political institutions in Ghana
Identify types of political institutions in the state, such as the executive, legislature, and judiciary
subtopics.keyConceptSummary: Precolonial Ghana had different political systems, including centralised states (like the Asante and Akwamu), non-centralised societies, and theocratic systems. Modern Ghana's political institutions — the executive, legislature, and judiciary — have roots in these earlier structures while also reflecting newer forms of governance.

subtopics.title: Citizenship and Human Rights
learningGoals: Examine the value of citizenship in nation-building
Discuss the various ways of acquiring citizenship in Ghana
Discuss the responsibilities of a Ghanaian citizen
Explain how citizens contribute to the country's development
subtopics.keyConceptSummary: Citizenship can be acquired in Ghana by birth, adoption, marriage, or registration. Being a good citizen means fulfilling responsibilities like obeying laws, protecting state property, paying taxes, and respecting national symbols — all of which contribute to the country's development.

subtopics.title: Indigenous Knowledge Systems
learningGoals: Identify indigenous medicinal plants used in the precolonial era to provide health care
Match medicinal plants to the diseases they cured in the precolonial era
Discuss the concept of traditional medicine and its importance
Investigate the processes and methods of indigenous medicinal practitioners in precolonial Ghana
subtopics.keyConceptSummary: Before modern medicine, Ghanaians relied on indigenous medicinal plants and traditional healers to treat illnesses. Traditional medicine practices, passed down through generations, remain an important part of Ghana's healthcare heritage today.

subtopics.keyConceptSummary: Socialisation is the process by which individuals learn the values, norms, and behaviours of their society. This happens through agencies like the family, school, and religious institutions, and agents like parents, teachers, and peers.

subtopics.title: European Encounter and the Slave Trade
learningGoals: Examine the coming of Europeans to the Gold Coast
Explore the early interactions between Europeans and the indigenous people
Describe the origins and development of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
Analyse the impact of the slave trade on Ghanaian society
subtopics.keyConceptSummary: European traders first arrived on the Gold Coast (present-day Ghana) seeking goods and later became involved in the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade. This trade had a devastating impact on Ghanaian society, including depopulation and the disruption of traditional social and economic structures.
